newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Pacific leaks continue to flow from Canberra.
newsitem.headline: Pacific leaks continue to flow from Canberra.

text.p: Already embarrassed by the loss of a top secret paper criticising its Pacific neighbours, Australia faced more discomfort on Wednesday with new leaks, including what appeared to be an angry foreign affairs department e-mail.

The latest leaks coincided with a government move to widen and upgrade an inquiry into circumstances surrounding publication last week of details of a 93-page AUSTEO -- Australian Eyes Only -- paper which contained a scathing assessment of South Pacific economies and leaders. AUSTEO is one of the highest security ratings.
A Reuters journalist found the document on a table in a public area at a summit earlier this month of economic ministers from the South Pacific, and reported on its contents last week.

As international criticism continued over the first gaffe, a copy what appeared to be a leaked foreign affairs department e-mail criticised "securocrats" in Prime Minister John Howard's intelligence office for believing in "a darker reality".
The inquiry will also include the leak of a second AUSTEO paper, details of which were reported on Wednesday by The Australian Associated Press (AAP).
Treasury Secretary Ted Evans said in a statement that the inquiry into the leaks has been turned over to Australia's Inspector-General of Intelligence, Ron McLeod.

A printed version of the e-mail, a memo criticising the scathing rundown of the Pacific by Howard's Office of National Assessments, was stapled to notes given to journalists at a foreign affairs department briefing on the results of elections in neighbouring Papua New Guinea.

"The fundamental problem seems to be that assessment agencies are disdainful of reality as presented by those of us out in the field and convinced that there is some darker reality which only they, from their securocrats' ivory tower, can detect and on which, as they jump at shadows, they insist on having the last word," said the memo.
The memo was signed Ian Lincoln and dated Wednesday.
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade lists an Ian Lincoln as Australia's deputy high commissioner to New Zealand.

A department spokeswoman told Reuters she could not comment on what appeared to be private correspondence between two people. She also would not comment on how the memo could have been attached to an official foreign affairs document.
The second AUSTEO document, a 39-page briefing for Treasurer Peter Costello, said neighbouring New Zealand's defence spending was "inadequate".
It detailed a cabinet strategy for Australian ministers to impress the need for bigger military spending on their Wellington counterparts at every opportunity.
The issue of New Zealand's defence spending was also touched on in the first document, which said New Zealand was becoming increasingly dependent on Australia for defence and trade.
Both AUSTEO documents were prepared for Costello for the summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the Australian resort town of Cairns.
The second paper, obtained by AAP, outlines Australian concern at New Zealand's defence budget.

"Inadequate NZ defence funding might mean Australia was seen to be accepting a disproportionate share of the bilateral burden," the paper said, adding that the latest draft of Wellington's upcoming defence review would still see long-term defence below 1990/91 levels.

The paper urged Costello to lobby New Zealand Treasurer and Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters -- labelled an opportunist and loose cannon in the first paper -- on the need for Wellington to take more responsibility for defence.

"Raising Australia's concerns with Winston Peters... will register this message with the cabinet member who holds the 'purse-strings' over competing NZ budget priorities -- especially social policy versus defence interests," it said.
